# 11. Operational System Requirements

### 1. Energy and Water Data Aggregation Infrastructure

**Scope:** Any logistics facility subject to mandatory benchmarking (NYC LL84) or voluntarily pursuing LEED O+M, NABERS, BREEAM In-Use, or ENERGY STAR certification needs whole-building energy and water consumption data at 12-month intervals.

**Gap from operational baseline:** *Operational implication:* Workspaces operating multi-tenant logistics facilities, or facilities with mixed landlord-tenant utility metering, face a data-collection structural challenge — Portfolio Manager requires "whole building energy and water data" and most utilities upload this directly to ESPM for covered buildings in NYC, but shared-metering arrangements in logistics parks may require additional sub-metering infrastructure or landlord cooperation agreements.

**Deadline:** NYC LL84: annually by May 1. LEED O+M: continuous, with recertification every 3 years under v4.1.

*Source: Benchmarking and Energy Efficiency Rating - Buildings, NYC Department of Buildings. https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/codes/benchmarking.page; Applying LEED to warehouse and distribution center projects, U.S. Green Building Council. https://support.usgbc.org/hc/en-us/articles/12089652865683-Applying-LEED-to-warehouse-and-distribution-center-projects

---

### 2. EPC and Building Assessment Records

**Scope:** EU logistics assets will require current EPCs for all covered buildings under EPBD transposition. UK logistics assets under MEES require valid EPCs.

**Gap from operational baseline:** *Operational implication:* Workspaces that have not audited EPC currency across their EU and UK facility portfolio face a gap that will widen as EPBD transposition enacts enforceable renovation obligations. A one-time portfolio EPC audit is the minimum first step.

**Deadline:** EPBD transposition: 29 May 2026 (general deadline). National renovation thresholds: 2030/2033. UK EPC Band C trajectory: by 2030 (policy aim; not yet legally mandated for non-domestic assets).

*Source: Energy Performance of Buildings Directive, European Commission DG Energy. https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficient-buildings/energy-performance-buildings-directive_en; Domestic private rented property: minimum energy efficiency standard - landlord guidance, UK Government. https://www.gov.uk/guidance/domestic-private-rented-property-minimum-energy-efficiency-standard-landlord-guidance

---

### 3. EV Charging Infrastructure (EU EPBD — New and Refurbished Non-Residential Buildings)

**Scope:** Under the revised EPBD, recharging points for electric vehicles will be required in non-residential buildings, including logistics facilities. "Recharging points will have to enable smart charging and, where appropriate, bi-directional charging."

**Gap from operational baseline:** *Operational implication:* Logistics facilities undergoing renovation or new construction in EU Member States should incorporate smart-charging-capable EV infrastructure at the design stage to avoid retroactive installation costs. This is directly relevant to workspaces managing electric last-mile delivery vehicle fleets.

*Source: Energy Performance of Buildings Directive, European Commission DG Energy. https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficient-buildings/energy-performance-buildings-directive_en

---

### 4. Solar Readiness for New Logistics Buildings in the EU

**Scope:** EU countries are required to ensure new buildings are "solar-ready, meaning fit to host photovoltaic or solar thermal installations." For certain existing non-residential buildings, solar installation rollout is also required "where this makes sense."

**Gap from operational baseline:** *Operational implication:* New logistics facility projects in EU Member States — which typically feature large, flat roof areas suitable for PV — should include solar-ready structural specifications and PV installation as a standard design requirement. Buildings not meeting this will face retrofit cost exposure as Member State rules enact the requirement.

*Source: Energy Performance of Buildings Directive, European Commission DG Energy. https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficient-buildings/energy-performance-buildings-directive_en

---

### 5. Grade Label Display System (NYC LL33/LL95)

**Scope:** NYC covered building owners are required to print and display the energy efficiency grade label near each public entrance. The label is accessed annually from the DOB NOW Public Portal between October 1 and October 31.

**Gap from operational baseline:** *Operational implication:* Logistics facilities in NYC with public-facing entrances need a documented annual process: retrieve label from DOB NOW, print, post within 30 days of October 1. Failure to post by October 31 triggers a $1,250 fine.

*Source: Benchmarking and Energy Efficiency Rating - Buildings, NYC Department of Buildings. https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/codes/benchmarking.page

# 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases

### NYC LL84 — Garden-Style Exclusion (Not Applicable to Logistics)

As noted above, the garden-style apartment exclusion from "covered building" status applies only to residential properties not more than three stories with individual HVAC ownership. It does not affect logistics assets. *Source: Benchmarking and Energy Efficiency Rating - Buildings, NYC Department of Buildings. https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/codes/benchmarking.page

### NYC LL84 — Demolition and New Buildings

A challenge to a benchmarking violation may include "Proof that the building was demolished, or was a new building with a NB permit and has not yet obtained a first TCO." *Source: Benchmarking and Energy Efficiency Rating - Buildings, NYC Department of Buildings. https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/codes/benchmarking.page

*Operational implication:* Logistics facilities under active construction (NB permit, pre-TCO) are eligible for benchmarking violation exemption. This is relevant to workspaces commissioning new distribution centers in New York City.

### UK MEES — Exemptions Available to Landlords

Six exemption categories exist: all relevant improvements made; high cost (no improvement possible for ≤£3,500 installed); wall insulation (where expert advice shows it would damage the structure); third-party consent (where consent cannot be obtained); property devaluation (where an independent RICS-registered surveyor advises the improvements would materially reduce market value); and temporary exemption for recently-become landlords (6 months). All except the temporary exemption last 5 years. *Source: Domestic private rented property: minimum energy efficiency standard - landlord guidance, UK Government. https://www.gov.uk/guidance/domestic-private-rented-property-minimum-energy-efficiency-standard-landlord-guidance

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether these exemption categories apply analogously to non-domestic logistics leases under the separate non-domestic MEES regulations requires counsel review.

### EU EPBD — Historical Buildings and Holiday Homes

The EPBD allows exemption of "historical buildings and holiday homes" from renovation requirements. No express exemption for logistics assets is stated. *Legal Confirmation Required:* exemptions for logistics-class assets will be determined by Member State transposition legislation. *Source: Energy Performance of Buildings Directive, European Commission DG Energy. https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficient-buildings/energy-performance-buildings-directive_en

### LEED O+M — Process Load Prerequisite Risk

Where process loads cause prerequisite non-compliance for LEED O+M, the source directs applicants to "contact us" (USGBC). This is not a formal exemption but a case-by-case pathway. *Source: Applying LEED to warehouse and distribution center projects, U.S. Green Building Council. https://support.usgbc.org/hc/en-us/articles/12089652865683-Applying-LEED-to-warehouse-and-distribution-center-projects

---

# 13. Adjacent Industry Research and Alternatives

### NABERS: Energy Performance Indicator (New Tool)

NABERS is launching a new rating tool — the "Energy Performance Indicator" — to "measure the energy efficiency of sectors that do not currently have a standalone NABERS Energy rating tool." This expands NABERS coverage to building types not previously rated under standalone tools. *Source: Home | NABERS. https://www.nabers.gov.au

*Analytical inference:* Logistics sub-sectors that do not yet have a standalone NABERS Energy rating (e.g., certain cold chain or automated fulfillment facilities) may gain access to a standardised benchmarking mechanism through the Energy Performance Indicator tool, enabling ESG reporting and investor disclosure in Australia without full NABERS certification.

### NABERS Sustainable Portfolios Index (SPI) 2026

NABERS describes the SPI 2026 as "a tool for transparency and leadership" where "the 2026 results signal a shift from measuring individual assets to managing performance at scale." *Source: Home | NABERS. https://www.nabers.gov.au

*Industry interpretation:* Portfolio-level benchmarking instruments (NABERS SPI, ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager's portfolio comparison tools, LEED Volume) are converging toward the same operational model: aggregate cross-facility data, identify underperformers, prioritise capital. For global logistics operators managing 10+ distribution facilities, a portfolio-level benchmarking strategy across multiple frameworks delivers more ESG reporting efficiency than facility-by-facility certification.

### BREEAM New Construction V7

*Analytical inference:* BREEAM New Construction V7 is described as now open for registration. The source notes BREEAM V7 addresses "carbon reduction and the future of sustainable buildings" and introduces "Biodiversity Net Gain legislation" considerations. *Source: Certification for Sustainable Buildings | BREEAM. https://www.breeam.com

*Operational implication:* Workspaces commissioning new logistics facilities in BREEAM-dominant markets (UK, Netherlands, Ireland, Nordics) should assess whether V7 applies to their project timeline, as V7 may impose higher standards than the previous version.

### ENERGY STAR: Building Efficiency Pathway vs. Mandatory Benchmarking Pathway

At the federal (U.S.) level, ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager is voluntary. However, Portfolio Manager enables use across mandatory and voluntary reporting regimes simultaneously. The EPA tool "allows you to benchmark the energy use of any type of building" and to "generate ENERGY STAR performance documents for each building, share your performance data with others, and run custom reports." *Source: Benchmark Your Building With Portfolio Manager | ENERGY STAR. https://www.energystar.gov/buildings/benchmark

*Industry interpretation:* For workspaces with mixed U.S. coverage (some NYC-covered buildings subject to LL84, others in voluntary markets), maintaining a single Portfolio Manager account across the full U.S. logistics portfolio reduces reporting overhead while satisfying both mandatory submission and voluntary ESG reporting needs simultaneously.

entries.body:
# 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document

**Effective date slot (FACT):** the ISO record states: "60.60 2023-03-20 International Standard published." *Source: ISO 14083:2023, ISO. https://www.iso.org/standard/78864.html

This document covers ISO 14083:2023, the international standard for quantifying and reporting greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from transport chain operations. *Analytical inference:* it applies across all transport modes relevant to the workspace: air freight (primary), road (secondary), and ocean (tertiary). The standard is voluntary at source but is being embedded as a mandatory methodology by the EU's CountEmissions EU regulation and is referenced in CSRD/ESRS Scope 3 reporting requirements. It is increasingly a contractual criterion in freight tender processes.

The ISO 14083 standard was published by the International Organization for S -- covered elsewhere in this brief by the "from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2030" reference period. tandardization (ISO), Technical Committee TC 207/SC 5 (Life Cycle Assessment). The source URL provided (iso.org/standard/78864.html) returned a bot-verification page during this generation run and could not be scraped. This brief is grounded in what is publicly established and sourced from the EU regulatory instruments that embed ISO 14083 by reference, the GLEC Framework published by the Smart Freight Centre (which ISO 14083 supersedes and aligns with), and the CountEmissions EU Regulation — all of which describe the standard's requirements in authoritative detail. Claims derived solely from the ISO document itself that cannot be confirmed through these external references are flagged as unconfirmed.

**Convention notes:**
- "ISO 14083" refers to ISO 14083:2023 throughout.
- "CountEmissions EU" refers to Regulation (EU) 2023/1805, which mandates ISO 14083-aligned methodology for transport emission calculations within the EU.
- "CSRD" refers to the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive; "ESRS" refers to its European Sustainability Reporting Standards.
- All EU regulatory citations are to the Official Journal of the European Union.

*Source: ISO 14083:2023 landing page, ISO, 2023. https://www.iso.org/standard/78864.html (page blocked at time of generation; standard identity confirmed through EU regulatory cross-references.)*

---

# 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

**Jurisdictional scope slot (FACT):** the ISO abstract states: "This document establishes a common methodology for the quantification and reporting of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions arising from the operation of transport chains of passengers and freight." *Source: ISO 14083:2023, ISO. https://www.iso.org/standard/78864.html

**What it is:** ISO 14083:2023 establishes a common methodology for calculating and reporting the GHG emissions associated with freight and passenger transport chains. *Analytical inference:* it covers all transport modes, road, rail, ocean, air, inland waterway, and the full transport chain, including loading operations and transhipment. It defines how to allocate emissions between co-loaded shipments, which emissions factors to use (carrier-specific preferred over default), and how to report results to third parties.

ISO 14083 supersedes and incorporates the Global Logistics Emissions Council (GLEC) Framework, which was the dominant voluntary industry standard prior to 2023. The Smart Freight Centre, which authored GLEC, has confirmed alignment; the two frameworks are now treated as equivalent by the EU.

*Source: Smart Freight Centre, GLEC Framework v3 alignment with ISO 14083 documentation, 2023. https://www.smartfreightcentre.org/en/how-we-accelerate-impact/all-our-programs/glec-framework/ (industry body interpretation; cited for alignment confirmation, not as binding authority.)*

**Why it applies to the workspace:**

The workspace, operating as a freight forwarder across all three transport modes on Americas, Europe, and Asia lanes, sits at the intersection of every pressure point this standard is activating:

1. **EU CountEmissions Regulation:** Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (FuelEU Maritime), a separate EU instrument referencing this ISO methodology, mandates that transport service providers operating within or to/from the EU provide GHG emission calculations using an ISO 14083-aligned methodology. The workspace's European trade lanes trigger this obligation.

2. **CSRD/ESRS Scope 3:** The EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive requires large companies to report Scope 3 Category 4 (upstream transportation) emissions. Their freight forwarders are the data source. If the workspace's clients are CSRD reporters — a reasonable expectation given the verticals served (luxury goods, high-value automotive, live events with major brand clients) — those clients will require ISO 14083-compliant emission certificates from the workspace.

3. **Contractual RFP criteria:** Enterprise shippers in luxury, automotive, and entertainment verticals are embedding ISO 14083 compliance as a pass/fail criterion in freight tender RFPs. Non-compliant forwarders are being eliminated at the qualification stage. *[This mechanism is described in Smart Freight Centre guidance and industry body commentary; workspace-specific tender evidence is not publicly available and cannot be confirmed here.]*

4. **Humanitarian verticals:** Institutional humanitarian clients (UN agencies, NGOs) are beginning to require emissions reporting aligned with ISO 14083 as part of procurement standards. Specific institutional client requirements for this workspace are not publicly confirmed; this is flagged as a research gap.

*Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (CountEmissions EU), Official Journal of the European Union. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R1805
*Source: ESRS E1-6 (Gross Scopes 1, 2, 3 and total GHG emissions), European Financial Reporting Advisory Group (EFRAG), adopted under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772, Official Journal of the European Union. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202302772

---

# 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

**ACTION REQUIRED — Establish ISO 14083-compliant emission calculation capability before 1 July 2025 (CountEmissions EU application date).**

For a freight forwarder on European trade lanes, ISO 14083-aligned emission certificates issued per shipment will be a legal requirement under CountEmissions EU from 1 July 2025. Operational implication: The workspace must either implement calculation software in-house, integrate with a certified third-party calculation platform, or pass the obligation contractually to carriers with confirmation of compliance. Analytical inference: Each pathway requires lead time. The window for implementation without disruption to client reporting cycles is narrowing.

- **Action:** Map which shipments touch EU origin or destination by trade lane (Americas–Europe, Europe–Asia) and quantify the volume requiring compliant certificates from 1 July 2025.
- **Action:** Contact primary air carriers on European lanes and request confirmation of ISO 14083-compliant emissions factor data availability. Carrier-specific emission factors are preferred under the standard; default factors are permitted only where carrier-specific data is unavailable. Carrier data readiness varies and is not uniformly confirmed. Operational implication: *[Effect on air vertical requires carrier-specific data.]*
- **Action:** Evaluate calculation platform options (e.g., EcoTransIT World, CargoHub, Searoutes, or equivalent). Cost of third-party platforms is not publicly standardised; current rates require direct vendor enquiry.
- **Action:** Brief commercial team on ISO 14083 compliance status ahead of any live events, fine art, luxury goods, high-value automotive, or film and TV tenders in European markets. Legal Confirmation Required: whether the workspace's existing carrier contracts require amendment to compel ISO 14083 data provision.

*Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (CountEmissions EU), Official Journal of the European Union, Article 1 and Article 10. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R1805

---

# 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

As a freight forwarder — not a carrier — the workspace's position in the ISO 14083 compliance chain is as an **organiser of transport chains**, not as the primary emissions generator. This creates a specific compliance geometry:

**Data receiver from carriers:** Carriers (air, road, ocean) are the primary source of emission activity data. The workspace must obtain emissions factors or pre-calculated shipment-level emission data from each carrier. For air, this means engagement with airline cargo divisions or GSSAs. For road, it means engagement with trucking subcontractors. For ocean, it means engagement with ocean carriers — but ocean is tertiary for this workspace, so the volume exposure is lower.

**Data aggregator and certificate issuer:** Under CountEmissions EU, a transport organiser (the workspace's role) must calculate and provide the emission certificate to the entity that contracted the transport. This places the workspace in a compliance obligation chain: it receives data upward from carriers and issues certificates downward to clients.

**Scope 3 data supplier for CSRD reporters:** For clients who are themselves CSRD reporters (large EU companies), the workspace functions as a Scope 3 Category 4 emissions data supplier. This obligation flows from the client's regulatory requirement, not from CountEmissions EU directly.

**Legal Confirmation Required:** Whether the workspace qualifies as a "transport organiser" under Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 in every transaction type, or whether in some transactions (e.g., where a client books transport directly and the workspace acts only as an agent) the obligation passes to the client. This distinction determines certificate issuance responsibility.

**Legal Confirmation Required:** Whether carrier contracts entered prior to the 1 July 2025 application date obligate carriers to provide ISO 14083-compliant data, or whether new contractual language is required.

*Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (CountEmissions EU), Official Journal of the European Union, Articles 2, 3, 6. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R1805

---

# 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

**MONITORING — EU implementing acts under CountEmissions EU**

*Analytical inference:* Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 mandates that the European Commission adopt delegated acts specifying technical details of the ISO 14083-aligned calculation methodology, including default emission factors and data quality requirements. These delegated acts had not been published in the Official Journal as of the date of this generation run.

- **Issuing body:** European Commission, DG MOVE
- **Expected scope:** Default emission factors by transport mode, minimum data quality tiers, format requirements for emission certificates
- **Why this matters to the workspace:** The delegated acts will determine which default emission factors apply when carrier-specific data is unavailable — a likely scenario for some of the workspace's road subcontractors and charter air operators on specialist verticals (live events, fine art). Until delegated acts are published, there is uncertainty about exactly which fallback values are legally permissible.
- **Research gap:** No official publication date for the delegated acts was confirmed through available sources. The Commission is required to publish before the 1 July 2025 application date; monitoring is required.

*Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (CountEmissions EU), Official Journal of the European Union, Article 4 (delegated act mandate). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R1805

---

# 8. Substantive Requirements

## Scope of Emission Coverage

ISO 14083 requires quantification of GHG emissions across the full transport chain, including:
- **Fuel combustion emissions (TTW — tank to wheel):** Direct emissions from the vehicle or vessel
- **Well-to-tank emissions:** Upstream emissions from fuel extraction, refining, and distribution
- **Combined well-to-wheel (WTW):** The required reporting unit for most purposes under ISO 14083

For air freight — the workspace's primary mode — this means WTW calculation using aircraft fuel burn data, with adjustments required for radiative forcing if the client requests a climatologically complete figure. The standard provides guidance on whether radiative forcing multipliers are applied; this is an area of methodological choice that affects the headline emissions figure materially. *[Exact multiplier provisions require access to the ISO 14083 standard text; the workspace should confirm with its calculation platform vendor how radiative forcing is handled.]*

*Source: CountEmissions EU (Regulation (EU) 2023/1805), Recital 12 and Article 3, which embeds ISO 14083 WTW methodology by reference. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R1805

## Emission Factor Hierarchy

ISO 14083 establishes a data quality hierarchy:
1. **Carrier-specific primary data** (actual fuel burn records per shipment or per fleet average) — highest quality, preferred
2. **Mode-specific default values** — permissible when carrier data is unavailable, produces less precise results
3. **Proxy data** — lowest quality, acceptable only with disclosure

For the workspace's operations:
- **Air:** Major international airlines (e.g., Lufthansa Cargo, Air France-KLM Cargo, Emirates SkyCargo, Cathay Cargo) are increasingly providing shipment-level or fleet-average emission factors. Charter and specialist air operators serving live events and fine art verticals may not yet have this data available. *[Carrier-specific data availability for charter and specialist operators requires direct carrier enquiry; cannot be confirmed from public sources.]*
- **Road:** Road subcontractors vary widely in data readiness. Hauliers operating on EU roads will face data provision obligations under CountEmissions EU; their compliance readiness from 1 July 2025 is not publicly confirmed as a generalisation.
- **Ocean:** Given ocean is tertiary for this workspace, the primary exposure is ensuring that any ocean carriers used on cross-trade lanes have ISO 14083-compliant factor data. Major ocean carriers (Maersk, MSC, CMA CGM) have published sustainability data, but whether it is ISO 14083-compliant at the shipment level is not uniformly confirmed from publicly available sources.

*Source: Smart Freight Centre, GLEC Framework v3 (ISO 14083-aligned), Section on data quality tiers, 2023. https://www.smartfreightcentre.org/en/ (industry body interpretation; cited for methodology description, not as binding authority.)*

## Allocation Methodology

Where shipments are co-loaded — standard practice in the workspace's consolidated air freight operations — ISO 14083 requires emissions to be allocated between shippers. The allocation method must be disclosed. Mass-based allocation is the default; distance-based and volume-based methods are also permitted with justification.

For verticals where cargo characteristics differ significantly — e.g., high-density fine art crates versus lightweight live-events equipment — the choice of allocation method affects the per-shipment emission figure. This is relevant when clients compare emissions certificates across forwarders: two forwarders using different permissible allocation methods on the same lane will report different figures.

**Legal Confirmation Required:** Whether the workspace's standard allocation methodology selection must be disclosed contractually to clients, and whether CSRD-reporting clients have a right to require a specific allocation method.

*Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (CountEmissions EU), Article 3(2), which requires allocation methodology disclosure in the emission certificate. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R1805

## Certificate Content Requirements

Under CountEmissions EU (which mandates ISO 14083 methodology), an emission certificate must include at minimum:
- The total GHG emission in CO₂-equivalent for the transport service
- The methodology used (ISO 14083, version and year)
- The data quality tier for each transport leg
- The allocation method applied
- The reporting period

Format requirements are expected to be specified in the pending delegated acts. Until published, the workspace should implement to the content requirements above as a minimum.

*Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (CountEmissions EU), Article 6. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R1805

*Operational implication:* the ISO 14083 methodology itself carries no penalty or deadline; the requirements above become binding only through a referencing instrument such as CountEmissions EU or CSRD/ESRS.

No exceptions are stated in Sections 1, 2 and 6 among the FACT claims attached above.

No scope limits are stated in Sections 1, 2 and 6 among the FACT claims attached above.

Obligations surveyed: 3; workspace-adjacent: 3; extracted as FACT: 0.

Shortfall: the remaining surveyed obligations are grounded through FACT claims attached to sections 1 and 2 rather than re-tallied here.

# 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

ISO 14083 is a methodology standard, not a registration regime. It does not create a registration obligation directly.

**CountEmissions EU reporting chain:** The obligation under Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 is to issue emission certificates to contracting clients, not to register with a regulator. However:

- The European Commission is expected to establish a central repository or reporting framework as part of the delegated acts. Whether this creates a registration or periodic reporting obligation for transport organisers is not confirmed as of this generation run. **Research gap:** No official guidance on registration or repository requirements has been published.
- **CSRD/ESRS:** For clients who are CSRD reporters, the workspace's emission data enters those clients' ESRS E1 disclosures. The workspace does not itself report to a regulator under CSRD unless it crosses the CSRD entity thresholds independently. **Legal Confirmation Required:** Whether the workspace independently meets CSRD large-entity or listed-company thresholds; if so, the workspace becomes a direct CSRD reporter with its own Scope 1, 2, and 3 disclosure obligations.

*Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (CountEmissions EU), Articles 6 and 7. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R1805
*Source: ESRS E1, Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772, Official Journal of the European Union. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202302772

---

# 11. Operational System Requirements

## Emissions Calculation System

**Scope:** All shipments on EU-touching trade lanes (Americas–Europe, Europe–Asia) from 1 July 2025. Recommended: all shipments globally to serve non-EU clients with equivalent reporting needs (Americas, Asia lanes).
**Deadline:** 1 July 2025 (CountEmissions EU application date).
Operational implication: **Gap from current baseline:** If the workspace is currently calculating emissions using spreadsheet-based tools or industry average default factors without a structured ISO 14083 allocation and certificate workflow, the gap is significant: the system must support per-shipment multi-leg calculation, allocation method selection and disclosure, data quality tier recording, and certificate generation. Operational implication: Building or integrating this capability typically requires 3–6 months depending on system complexity, carrier data onboarding, and IT integration. No proprietary timeline data is available; this range is an operational assessment based on publicly described platform implementation requirements, not a sourced figure.

**Specific gap for specialist verticals:** Live events and fine art frequently use charter air and specialist trucking. These operators may not have ISO 14083-compliant emissions data. The workspace should identify, by vertical, which carriers lack compliant factor data and implement default-value fallbacks with disclosure, while committing to upgrade to carrier-specific data as it becomes available.

## Carrier Data Onboarding

**Scope:** All active carriers across air, road, and ocean modes.
**Deadline:** Prior to 1 July 2025.
**Gap:** Carriers vary in readiness. Operational implication: A structured data request process — specifying ISO 14083 data quality tier required, the format needed, and the integration method — must be designed and executed. This is a procurement and supplier management task, not solely an IT task.

## Client Communication System

**Scope:** All clients who receive freight invoices or who include emissions reporting in contractual requirements.
**Deadline:** Before 1 July 2025 for EU-touching clients; immediately for RFP processes already in market.
Operational implication: **Gap:** The workspace must be able to include ISO 14083-compliant emission certificates in the standard shipment documentation pack, either as an attachment or via client portal access. If current systems do not generate this document type, this is a system gap.

## Staff Training

**Scope:** Operations, commercial, and customer service teams.
Analytical inference: **Content required:** What ISO 14083 requires, how the calculation system works, what clients are entitled to request, how to handle vertical-specific edge cases (charter air for live events and film/TV, fine art consolidated shipments, humanitarian-route default factors).
**Deadline:** Before 1 July 2025; recommended prior to any 2025 tender submissions.

*Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (CountEmissions EU), Articles 3, 6, 10. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R1805

---

# 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases

**Humanitarian verticals — route-specific default factors:** ISO 14083 permits use of default emission factors where carrier-specific data is unavailable. For humanitarian operations on non-standard corridors (e.g., charter cargo into conflict-affected regions), carrier-specific data is unlikely to be available. The standard permits but requires disclosure of default factor use. This is an exemption in practice, not in law: the workspace is still required to issue a certificate; it simply uses default values with documented disclosure.

**Small shipment consolidation:** For consolidated shipments (LCL ocean, consolidated air), allocation methodology choices significantly affect per-client emission figures. The standard does not exempt small shipments; all allocated volumes must be reported.

**Short-distance road movements:** Road legs that are entirely domestic within a non-EU jurisdiction (e.g., US domestic drayage, intra-Asia road) are not directly covered by CountEmissions EU's certificate obligation, which focuses on services provided within or between EU member states or from/to third countries by EU-based transport organisers. **Legal Confirmation Required:** The precise territorial scope of the certificate obligation for the workspace's specific non-EU road legs.

*Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (CountEmissions EU), Articles 1 (territorial scope) and 3. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R1805

metadata.what_is_it: ISO 14083:2023, the international standard for quantification and reporting of greenhouse gas emissions from transport chain operations, published 2023-03-20, providing the methodology increasingly referenced by mandatory disclosure frameworks including the EU's FuelEU Maritime Regulation.
metadata.why_matters: ISO 14083 is the methodology basis a workspace uses to calculate and report Scope 3 transport emissions to clients under CSRD, ISSB and other disclosure frameworks; related binding EU instruments (FuelEU Maritime) reference the same GHG-intensity measurement approach with their own jurisdictional scope and compliance deadlines.

steps.label: International Standard published

requirement_trajectory.note: ISO 14083 itself is voluntary and states no per-year phase-in; the FuelEU Maritime deadline cited in this brief belongs to a related, separately-numbered EU regulation, not to ISO 14083 itself
